newsitem.title: UK: Summary of Monday's events in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Summary of Monday's events in UK election.

text.p: The following is a summary of Monday's main events in the British election campaign:
WAR REPORTER STEPS INTO FRAY
Veteran war reporter Martin Bell emerged as the awaited anti-sleaze candidate to stand against defiant Conservative Neil Hamilton, and said he would rather be facing bullets.
"I think it's going to be the shortest career in British political history," Bell, who pledges to stand down if Hamilton resigns, told Reuters.
"I would much rather run the trench lines... or tackle Sniper's Alley (in Sarajevo) in my armoured vehicle Miss Piggy than be going through this. I really would."
HAMILTON VOWS TO STAY ON
Hamilton, whose party will decide at a meeting on Tuesday whether to reselect him, remained adamant that he would not bow to demands that he resign over "cash-for-questions" allegations.
But Hamilton stayed hidden from view, relying on his wife to issue his latest statement of defiance.
"If you think we are going to chicken out three-and-a-half weeks before polling day, you are all mad," Christine Hamilton declared.
BLAIR PLEDGES ON THE ECONOMY
On the party leaders' campaign trail, Labour's Tony Blair again sought to reassure business leaders that the health of the economy would be assured under his rule.
Britain had been on an economic rollercoaster since the Conservatives took power in 1979, with each boom being followed by bust, he said.

"This instability is not a natural phenomenon visited upon us by the Almighty. It has been caused, to be frank, by the least competent management of any western economy in the past two decades," he said.
CONSERVATIVES ON ATTACK

The Conservatives returned to the attack over what they called policy u-turns by Labour. Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke seized on his shadow Gordon Brown's refusal to rule out privatisation of the air traffic control system and media suggestions Labour would sell off other government assets.

"The opposition party changes its policy from day to day. What it shows is a party that has no set policies, that has no convictions, that has no principles and they are now making it up day by day as they go along," Clarke told reporters.
SCOTTISH NATIONALISTS UNVEIL PLANS
In Edinburgh, the Scottish Nationalist Party (SNP) unveiled its manifesto, pledging lower taxes and claiming an independent Scotland would be the world's eighth richest nation.

"Yes we can become independent and pay our way in the world. Yes we can have a first class health service, improve our schools and colleges, create jobs, build homes and look after our elderly and vulnerable," said SNP leader Alex Salmond.

The manifesto was immediately scorned by Scottish Minister Michael Forsyth, who called the SNP "the Disneyworld alternative in this election because they are creating expectations which cannot be realised."
UK INDEPENDENCE PARTY LAUNCHES PLANS
The U.K. Independence Party also set out its single-issue election stall with a ferocious attack on the European Union.

"It is the most bizarre set of undemocratic, unaccountable, incompetent, financially-profligate institutions that the world has ever seen," party leader Alan Sked told reporters at the launch of the UKIP's first national election manifesto. "The only way is out."
